topics: 🍷 Rabbi Meir's Retroactive Designation — drinking Samaritan wine before separating teruma and tithes
🚫 Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon Object — why they reject relying on a future separation
🔑 Rabbi Yochanan's Resolution — 'this purse will not be exempt from consecration' points to the LAST coin
⚖️ Purses and Wine Barrels Compared — why one case allows relying on the future and the other does not
🏁 The Tractate Concludes — Meilah's journey from disqualified offerings to the peruta in an agent's purse

overview.title: 📖 Overview: One Last Challenge, and the Tractate's Close
overview.subtitle: Meilah 22a
overview.hebrewSource: הַדְרָן עֲלָךְ הַשָּׁלִיחַ שֶׁעָשָׂה שְׁלִיחוּתוֹ וּסְלִיקָא לַהּ מַסֶּכֶת מְעִילָה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Rav Pappa offers a third version of Reish Lakish's challenge to Rabbi Yoḥanan, this time from a mishna in Demai about wine purchased from Samaritans before Shabbat: Rabbi Meir permits designating future portions as teruma and tithes and drinking immediately, relying on that future separation, while Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon forbid it. If Rabbi Meir's retroactive designation is valid, shouldn't the mishna about a consecrated peruta lost somewhere in a purse likewise allow drinking down to the last coin without concern, the way the earlier version about bulls assumed the finer of two animals was meant? Rabbi Yoḥanan again resolves the difficulty the same way as before, showing the mishna's language about 'this purse will not be exempt from consecration' picks out the specific, final coin. With that, the daf closes with the formula ending tractate Meilah.

slides.title: 🍷 Rabbi Meir's Method for Samaritan Wine
slides.subtitle: Designating future separations to drink immediately, before Shabbat
rows: 'Two log that I will separate in the future are teruma' (out of 100 log)
Teruma is designated in advance, at the standard 1/50 rate
'Ten log [of the remainder] are first tithe'
'Nine log are second tithe' (1/10 of the remainder)
Ma'aser sheni designated, then desacralized by transferring its sanctity to money
Relying on the future separation he will actually perform later

callout.label: This is Rabbi Meir's opinion alone:
callout.text: Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon all prohibit this approach — they reject relying on a designation that has not yet actually been carried out.

slides.title: 🚫 Does Retroactive Designation Really Work?
slides.subtitle: Rav Pappa's version of Reish Lakish's challenge to Rabbi Yoḥanan

lines.speaker: Rav Pappa (for Reish Lakish)
lines.text: Rabbi Meir permits drinking now and separating teruma/tithes LATER, relying on a future designation — doesn't that prove retroactive designation works generally? If so, why does the mishna about a lost consecrated peruta require spending down the WHOLE purse, rather than simply relying on a future separation?

lines.speaker: Implicit reply
lines.text: Even Rabbi Meir's own method only works when he specifies 'that which I will separate in the FUTURE' — a concrete, upcoming act. In the purse case, by contrast, the consecrated coin is already unidentifiably mixed in NOW — there's no future act of separation to rely on.

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan's resolution
lines.text: The mishna's latter clause is understood through its specific wording: 'this purse will not be exempt from consecration' — meaning the person intended the very LAST coin remaining to be the consecrated one, not an as-yet-undetermined future portion.

slides.title: 🔑 The Wording That Resolves Everything
slides.subtitle: 'This purse will not be exempt from consecration'
slides.hebrewSource: סֵיפָא דְּמַתְנִיתִין בְּאוֹמֵר ״לֹא יִפָּטֵר כִּיס זֶה מִן הַהֶקְדֵּשׁ״
slides.label: The key phrase:
slides.text: Rabbi Yoḥanan resolves each version of Reish Lakish's challenge — whether comparing the purse mishna to bulls, to log-measures of wine, or now to the Demai teaching on Samaritan wine — the same way. When the mishna's latter clause says one is not liable for me'ilah until the ENTIRE purse is spent, it is describing someone who explicitly framed his consecration as 'this purse will not be exempt' — a phrase that identifies the last, final coin as the consecrated one, regardless of when it turns up. That is fundamentally different from an open-ended 'the consecrated coin is somewhere in here.'

slides.title: ⚖️ Two Cases, One Real Difference
slides.subtitle: Why Rabbi Meir's wine ruling doesn't actually contradict the purse mishna

boxes.title: Samaritan Wine (R' Meir)
items: Declares a SPECIFIC future act: 'the two log I will separate LATER'
The designation names a concrete quantity, to be actualized going forward
Relies on a real future separation — a defined, upcoming event

boxes.title: The Purse (Rabbis, first clause)
items: 'A peruta IN this purse is consecrated' — no specific coin identified
Any coin spent might be THE coin — no future act pending
Liability begins with the first coin spent, per the Rabbis

callout.label: Where they converge:
callout.text: Only when the purse-case wording shifts to 'this purse will not be exempt' does it functionally resemble Rabbi Meir's case — designating the LAST remaining item, much like designating a specific future portion.

slides.title: 🏁 Tractate Meilah Concludes
slides.subtitle: From the Temple altar to a coin in an agent's pocket

steps.content: 1️⃣ Opened with offerings disqualified by place or time, and Rabbi Yehoshua's principle: a 'period of fitness for the priests' removes an item from me'ilah
2️⃣ Traced me'ilah through blood, libations, ashes, milk, eggs, and produce — precisely defining where consecration's reach begins and ends
3️⃣ Established which items combine to reach the liability threshold, and clarified when damage, benefit, or both are required
4️⃣ Closed with the law of agency — who bears liability when a messenger acts faithfully, partially, or not at all

callout.label: The closing formula:
callout.text: הַדְרָן עֲלָךְ הַשָּׁלִיחַ שֶׁעָשָׂה שְׁלִיחוּתוֹ וּסְלִיקָא לַהּ מַסֶּכֶת מְעִילָה — 'We shall return to you, [the chapter of] the agent who performed his agency, and thus concludes tractate Meilah.'

summary.principle: Retroactive designation only works when it names a concrete, specific future act — like Rabbi Meir's defined portion of wine to be separated later — while an unidentified consecrated coin merely 'somewhere in the purse' requires spending everything before liability is certain, unless the declaration itself points to the final remaining coin.

flowSteps.content: 🍷 Rabbi Meir permits drinking wine now, relying on a specific future teruma/tithe designation
🚫 Rabbi Yehuda, Yosei, and Shimon reject relying on any as-yet-unperformed separation
🔑 Rabbi Yochanan: the purse mishna's stricter clause describes someone who named the LAST coin specifically

columns.content: ⚖️ A defined future portion (wine) can be relied upon in advance
⚖️ An unidentified coin 'somewhere in the purse' cannot — until the wording specifies the last one

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: tractate Meilah closes having shown that precision — of wording, of timing, of category — governs every boundary of consecrated property

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Meir, how may a person permissibly drink wine purchased from Samaritans before separating teruma and tithes?
o: He may never drink it under any circumstances
By declaring in advance a specific future separation (e.g., 'two log I will separate later are teruma') and relying on that designation to drink immediately
By drinking only after actually removing all teruma and tithes
By asking a priest for special permission
quiz.e: Rabbi Meir permits designating specific future portions as teruma and tithes and relying on that declaration to drink the wine right away, before physically performing the separation.

quiz.q: Which Sages disagree with Rabbi Meir's method of retroactive designation for the Samaritan wine, and what is their basic objection?
o: No one disagrees; it is universally accepted
Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon prohibit it, rejecting reliance on a designation that has not yet actually been carried out
Only Rabbi Akiva disagrees, for unrelated reasons
The Rabbis agree but require a different order of separation
quiz.e: The mishna in Demai records that Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon all forbid relying on a future, not-yet-performed act of separation.

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Yoḥanan resolve the apparent contradiction between Rabbi Meir's wine ruling and the purse mishna's requirement to spend the entire purse before certainty of me'ilah?
o: He says the two cases are unrelated and cannot be compared at all

He explains that the purse mishna's stricter clause refers to someone who said 'this purse will not be exempt from consecration,' meaning he specifically intended the LAST coin, similar to naming a specific future portion
He rules that Rabbi Meir's opinion is rejected entirely
He says the purse case always follows the lenient Rabbi Meir approach
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan consistently resolves each version of this challenge by pointing to the specific wording 'this purse will not be exempt,' which identifies a definite final coin, paralleling Rabbi Meir's defined future portion.

quiz.q: What is the crucial difference between Rabbi Meir's wine declaration and the basic case of 'a peruta IN this purse is consecrated' (where the Rabbis require spending the whole purse)?
o: There is no real difference between them
Rabbi Meir's declaration names a specific, defined future act of separation, while 'a peruta in this purse' does not identify any particular coin, leaving every expenditure uncertain
The wine case involves a much larger sum of money
The purse case only applies to gold coins
quiz.e: Rabbi Meir's method relies on a concrete, defined future action, whereas the basic purse declaration leaves the identity of the consecrated coin genuinely unknown until the entire purse is exhausted.

quiz.q: What Hebrew formula marks the conclusion of tractate Meilah on this daf?
o: 'Baruch Hashem le'olam, amen ve'amen'
'הַדְרָן עֲלָךְ הַשָּׁלִיחַ שֶׁעָשָׂה שְׁלִיחוּתוֹ וּסְלִיקָא לַהּ מַסֶּכֶת מְעִילָה' — 'We shall return to you, [the agent who performed his agency], and thus concludes tractate Meilah'
'Siyum masechet Menachot'
There is no closing formula; the tractate simply stops
quiz.e: The daf ends with the traditional 'hadran' formula naming the final chapter's opening words, followed by the explicit statement that tractate Meilah has concluded.
